title: Chapter 52: Lot 41, Part 5 of 5: Crown Walk
html:
The back door was locked, and Lyra had the only key to the front.
So they went round. Through the stable yard, past the dark coach-house where her father's carriage had stood and did not stand now. Past the harness room, with its door hanging open on one hinge and the smell of old leather still coming out of it after two years. Past the pump, frozen, with a long icicle hanging from its spout to the stone trough below like a glass rope. Along the narrow flagged passage at the side of the house, between the house wall and the garden wall, where the snow had drifted knee-deep and nobody had walked for two winters. Through the little iron gate at the end of it, which Tibbs opened with the second key on his ring.
And out onto Crown Walk.
It was very quiet. It was past midnight on Midwinter Eve, and every house on the Walk was dark except one, at the far end, where somebody's servants were still up, and a single window glowed yellow on the top floor. The snow lay smooth and white on the pale stone slabs of the pavement, that her grandfather had paid a third of. The lamps were lit, the gas lamps, the city's lamps, burning with their soft steady white-blue flame behind their glass. Polly paid for the gas, Corin had said last night. Lyra did not look at them.
She looked at the house.
It stood back from the street behind its railings and its little front garden, tall and narrow and dark. Four floors and the attics. Pale stone, gone gray with two winters of soot. Every window shuttered. The shutters were green, or had been. They were gray now too. Snow on the sills. Snow on the roof. Snow on the stone girl in the middle of the garden, who stood on her low stone plinth with her stone jug on her shoulder, pouring nothing into a stone basin full of snow, and had done for two years.
The steps went up to the front door. Five of them. Lyra had sat on the third one with Rowan in the summers, eating cherries and spitting the stones into the garden. She did not remember that. Oren had told her. She went up them now, in the snow, with the great black key in both her gloved hands.
The door was dark green, with brass on it, gone brown. A brass letter-plate. A brass bell-pull, with a handle like a small hand. And in the middle of the door, at the height of a man's face, a pale square, a little lighter than the green around it, with four small holes at its corners. Where the knocker had been. The brass hand holding a ball.
She put the key in the lock.
It went in hard. It had not been turned for two years. She turned it, and it would not go, and she put both hands on the bow and turned it again, harder. And from deep inside the door there came a sound, a heavy slow grinding click, like something old waking up and not wanting to. And the key turned. And the door moved, a little, inward, under her hand.
Oren, on the step behind her, with a child in his good arm, said nothing at all.
She pushed it open.
The cold came out first. A deep, still, shut-up cold, colder than the street, the cold of a house where no fire has been lit for two winters. It smelled of dust. And damp. And, very faintly, under the dust, of beeswax, and old wood, and something else, something she knew and could not name for a moment, something sweet and dry, like dried rose petals in a bowl.
And then she could name it. It was the house. That was all. It was just the smell of the house. Her house. The way it had always smelled, every day of her life, under everything, and she had never noticed it until she had lost it.
She stood on the threshold and could not move.
Tibbs came up beside her with a lamp. He held it up, over her shoulder, into the dark.
And there was the hall.
It was big, and square, and very high, going up the whole height of the house, with the stairs climbing round it on three sides, up and up, landing after landing, to a round window at the top that let in no light now because it was shuttered too. The floor was black and white marble, in squares, like a chessboard. She had played hopscotch on it, on the white squares only, until her governess caught her. The walls were pale green, with white plaster on the ceiling in the shape of leaves and flowers, and a great dark empty hook in the middle of the ceiling where the chandelier had hung. It had been sold at the auction. Everything had been sold at the auction, Oren had told her. The pictures. The carpets. The clocks. Her mother's harp. Everything the Duke had not bought himself, to keep.
And the Duke had bought the furniture. The big things. She could see them now, as Tibbs moved the lamp. Shapes. Under sheets. Great white shapes all round the edges of the hall, in the dark, like a crowd of ghosts standing very still against the walls, waiting. A long shape that was the hall table. A tall shape that was the clock that had stood at the foot of the stairs, that her father wound every Sunday night. A round shape that was the chair where Bertram sat to wait for the door. All of them under their white sheets, gray with two years of dust.
And the stairs.
She looked at them for a long time.
Wide shallow stairs of dark polished wood, going up from the black and white floor in a long curve, with a banister of the same dark wood on curved white iron rails. The bottom step was very wide, wider than the rest, curving out at the end in a sweep like the edge of a shell. And on that bottom step, every Midwinter, on the night of her father's reception, a thin pink smiling man in gold spectacles had stood with a little round silver box, and held it out to two children in their nightgowns peeping through the banisters, and said One each, now. Only one. And don't tell your mother.
Mr. Peppermint.
She made herself look away.
"My lady," said Oren behind her, very low. "The child's cold."
She went in.
And the others came in behind her, one by one, out of the snow. Oren with a child in his arm. Tibbs with the lamp. Mrs. Doyle with two. Rose with Tom and the baby on her back. Abner, black as his cart, carrying a girl of five as gently as if she were made of eggshell. The Duke's two farm men, big silent countrymen in smocks, who had not said a word all night, each with a child. And behind them, the next ones, and the next. Up the five steps. Across the threshold. Into the cold dark hall with its white ghosts and its black and white floor.
And Lyra, in the middle of the hall, with the great black key still in her hand, turned round in the lamplight and said, in a clear steady voice that did not sound like hers at all, the voice of her mother giving orders in this hall to a house full of servants:
"The nursery. Top floor. Up the stairs, all the way, and turn left. There's a fire there, the biggest one in the house. Tibbs, the coal is in the cellar, under the kitchen, where Father's man left it. Abner, can you find it? Mrs. Doyle, the blankets are in the long press on the second floor landing, forty-one of them, Oren knows. Rose, the kitchen is through the green door at the back, there's a range, and the cistern is under the yard, there'll be a pump in the scullery. We need fires. In every room on the top floor, and the second. And water hot. And broth. Silas said broth."
She stopped. They were all looking at her.
"Please," said Lyra.
And they went.
The house woke up round her.
She stood at the foot of the stairs and listened to it happen. Feet on the stairs. Doors opening, upstairs, one after another, with long groans, for the first time in two years. Voices, high up, calling to each other. Mrs. Doyle saying Saints, the dust. The rattle of the shutters coming down, in the rooms above, one window and then another, and pale snow-light coming in where there had been none. Abner's heavy feet going down the back stairs to the cellar, and then the long roaring rattle of coal going into a scuttle. Like a drum roll. Like the chute at the palace.
And from the top of the house, faint, from the nursery, from the room at the very top on the left where she had slept until she was twelve, the first crackle of a fire being lit.
She put her hand on the banister. The dark wood was cold and smooth under her glove. Dusty. She could feel the dust through the thin gray kid.
Oren came down the stairs. Slowly. He had carried the last of his children up. His arm was empty. He stopped on the bottom step, the wide one, the one shaped like the edge of a shell, and looked at her.
"He's in the library, my lady," he said. "Mister Vane. On the long sofa by the fire, under the sheet. I've lit it. The fire." He paused. "I put him in the library because it's got the biggest fire on the ground floor, and because it's got no mirrors. The doctor's woman said he wasn't to look in anything shiny."
"Thank you, Oren."
He did not like being thanked. He did not say anything. He looked round the hall instead. At the ghosts under their sheets. At the black and white floor. At the empty hook in the ceiling where the chandelier had been. And at the front door, standing open still, with the snow blowing in across the marble in a thin white fan.
He went and shut it.
He shut it the way he had shut it every night for twenty-two years. Last thing. After her father went up. Lyra watched him do it. He put his good hand flat on the dark green wood and pushed, slowly, until it met the frame. And then he put out his hand to her, without looking, the way a man puts out his hand for a thing he has always been given.
She put the great black key in it.
And Oren Vance turned the key in the lock of the house on Crown Walk, slowly, until the heavy slow grinding click came from deep inside the door. And took it out. And held it for a moment in his big hand, feeling the weight of it.
Then he gave it back to her.
"All's well, my lady," he said.
Forty-Seven
The nursery was at the very top of the house, at the end of the passage on the left, under the roof, and it was exactly as she had left it when she was twelve.
That was the strange thing. Everything else in the house had been taken, or covered, or sold. But nobody had bothered with the nursery. Nobody at the auction had wanted a nursery. So it was all still there, under the dust, in the light of the fire that Abner had lit in the big grate and that was roaring now, red and gold, throwing shadows up the sloping walls.
It was a long low room with a sloping ceiling, because it was under the roof, so that you could only stand up straight in the middle of it. Two dormer windows looked out over the back of the house, over the stable yard and the Mews Road and the roofs beyond. The walls were papered with a pattern of small blue birds on branches, faded now to the color of skimmed milk, with a damp brown stain in one corner where the roof had leaked one winter. The floor was bare boards, painted white, worn gray down the middle where children had run up and down. A rocking horse stood by the window, a big dapple-gray one with a real horsehair tail, gone thin, and one glass eye missing. There was a low table, scarred all over with pencil marks and knife marks and the rings of a thousand cups of milk. There was a shelf of books, and a box of wooden soldiers, and a doll's house with its front swung open and all its tiny furniture tipped over inside, as if a very small earthquake had happened in it a long time ago.
And against the wall by the door, three small chairs.
Three. In a row. Little wooden chairs with rush seats, painted white once. The paint was chipped. One had an L carved into its back, crooked, with a penknife. One had an R. And one had nothing. Its back had been sanded smooth, carefully, a long time ago, so that you could see the pale bare wood under the paint in a square where something had been.
On the shelf above the chairs, three cups. Children's cups, white china, with a blue band round the rim. Two of them had names painted on them in blue. Lyra. Rowan. The third had been scratched. All over. Round and round the place where a name should have been, until there was nothing there but a gray blur of fine scratches in the glaze, like frost on a window.
And on the wall beside the door, the height chart.
Lines in pencil, on the faded blue birds, going up from the floor. Each with a date beside it, in her mother's hand, small and quick and leaning back a little, the way foreign hands lean. Two columns. L. on the left, going up from very low, a baby's height, to the height of a girl of twelve. R. on the right, going up from lower still. And between them, a third column. Shorter. It began higher than the others, at the height of a child of two, and went up five lines, to the height of a child of six or so, and then stopped. And at the top of it, where a letter should have been, a deep rough gouge in the plaster, as if somebody had dug the letter out with the point of a knife.
Lyra had seen it in the autumn. With Corin, by the light of one candle, on the night they first came to look at the shut house. She had stood in front of it in the dark with a candle and not understood it. She did not understand it now.
She did not look at it long.
The room was full of children.
They lay on the floor, on the gray blankets from the crypt and the wool ones from the long press, in rows, in front of the fire. They lay on the window seats. Two of them lay in the old nursery beds, the two small iron beds against the far wall under the sloping roof, with their white iron rails and their brass knobs gone dull. Rose was kneeling by the fire with a pan of water heating on the coals. Mrs. Doyle was going down the rows with a cup and a spoon, saying the names. Bet was sitting on the floor with her back against the rocking horse, and Kit Flynn's head in her lap, and his wooden spoon held in his fist against her knee. She was asleep. So was he.
And in the small iron bed nearest the fire, the one on the left, the one with the dent in the brass knob where a girl of seven had once hit it with a wooden sword, Polly lay with her eyes open, watching the flames.
It was Lyra's bed.
She had not decided to put Polly in it. Somebody else had. Mrs. Doyle, probably, who did not know whose bed it had been. It did not matter. Lyra went and sat down on the edge of it, very carefully, the way you sit on the edge of a bed where somebody is ill. The old iron springs creaked under her, the way they had always creaked. She had forgotten that. She had forgotten the creak.
Polly's eyes came off the fire and onto her face.
Lyra took out Silas's bundle of pages from the doctor's bag, which she had carried up all four flights of stairs and would not put down. She found the page. The first one. Polly. Six. Hook Lane, thought to be. Mother not known. Hums.
She read it out loud. Softly. All of it. Every line of Silas's long thin sloping hand. How much Polly could eat, and how, and when. That she liked to be on her left side. That she was frightened of the dark and must always have a lamp. That she had blinked on Thursday. That she had looked at the lady, which was Lyra. And at the bottom, added later, in a different ink, very small:
Saturday. Hummed three notes, twice. Heard it from the harvester. She CAN hear. I should have known it. J. S.
And under that, in Lyra's own hand, because she had added it herself on Saturday night, in the crypt, before Silas went out on the step:
Saturday, ninth bell. A fourth note.
She stopped.
Polly was looking at her.
"Your name's Polly," said Lyra. "You're in my house. On the Hill. In my bed. It's Midwinter. Nobody is going to give you any sweets."
Polly looked at her.
And very softly, so softly that Lyra was not sure for a moment that she had heard it at all, a breath with a shape in it came out of the small gray face on the pillow. Three notes. Going up.
And a fourth.
And then, after a long pause, while the fire crackled and Mrs. Doyle went on down the rows with her spoon saying the names, a fifth.
And stopped.
Lyra sat on the edge of her own old bed and did not breathe.
Then she got out the pencil, the stub of pencil she kept in the list pocket of her mother's gown with the fifth letter and the Lady's list, and she wrote at the bottom of Polly's page, under her own line, in her own small quick hand:
Sunday. Midwinter Eve. Crown Walk. My bed. A fifth note.
And she put the page back in the bundle, and the bundle back in the bag.
Later, much later, when the second bell after midnight had rung across the city and the fires were burning in every room on the top floor and the second, and the broth was made, and Mrs. Doyle had gone down the rows twice with her spoon and come back and sat down on the floor by the fire and gone to sleep with her mouth open, Lyra went down one floor. To the room at the front of the house on the second floor, over the front door, with the two tall windows.
Her mother's room.
She did not go far into it. There was nothing in it. Everything had been sold. There was only a big pale square on the floor where the carpet had been, and a pale shape on the wall where the looking-glass had hung, and the two tall windows, shuttered. And the smell. Very faint. Dried rose petals in a bowl. It was strongest in here. It had always been strongest in here.
She went to the left-hand window and opened the shutter.
It was stiff. It squealed. She pushed it back against the wall, and the cold came in through the glass, and the light. The white-blue light of the gas lamps on Crown Walk, steady behind their glass, all the way along the street, on both sides. And above the roofs opposite, to the left, the glow of the Crescent. The long white curve of it, round the top of the Hill. Every lamp lit. All night. Every night. The whole Hill shining softly in the dark under the snow, like something precious kept in a case.
The city pays for the gas.
She looked at it for a long time.
Then she counted.
She did not mean to. She just did. She stood at her mother's window on Midwinter Eve with her gloved hands on the cold sill and counted the children in her house, the way her father had counted the silver on Sunday nights, the way Lucian counted steps. The ones on the top floor, in the nursery. The ones in the rooms along the passage. The ones on the second floor, in the rooms off the landing where Mrs. Doyle had made up beds out of the long press. She had them all in her head. She had carried every one of them up the stairs or watched them carried.
Forty-seven.
Forty-seven in the house on Crown Walk, behind a shut door, on the Hill, where nobody ever looked.
And four in the crypt of Saint Bride's, by the north brazier, with an old woman called Hannah holding their hands.
And one tall tired doctor with crooked spectacles, somewhere in the dark across the river, in a white room, having his little talk.
And one man downstairs in her father's library, on the long sofa by the fire, under a white sheet, with a stranger's face setting on him like plaster, who would get up in the morning and put on another man's gold coat and go to the Bourse.
And one old man in a chair by the fire in an inn at the end of the Lantern Bridge, writing about the weather in a new book, with a circle by his name.
And on a river somewhere to the north, past the last lamp, in the dark, a red light going upstream.
She stood at the window and held all of them in her head at once. It was very heavy. Heavier than the great black key. She did not put any of them down.
Below her, on the steps of the house, the snow had begun to fall again. Softly. Covering the marks of all their feet.
Midwinter, Lyra thought. It's Midwinter now.
And she shut the shutter, and went down to the library, to sit with Corin.
